transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Democrats and Republicans are spending heavily in U.S. House districts,
where President Trump comfortably won in 2024.
And NPR analysis of campaign spending finds dozens of races that are newly competitive.
NPR's Stephen Fowler explains.
Some competitive districts aren't surprising, like places that voted for one party for president
and the other for Congress.
And there are those districts decided by a small number of votes in 2024.
But this is 2026, where an unpopular president, rising prices,
and a general anti-incumbency vibe from the electorate means competitive districts stretch
into conservative territory.
Between the Democrats and Republicans' House campaign arm and spending from Trump-aligned
super PACs, we're talking over 90 districts on their radars.
And about 60, where the parties are investing serious money.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
New documents made public this week show that as part of President Trump's
broad search for election crimes, the federal government has investigated
nonprofit groups that register voters as well.
As NPR's Miles Parks reports, these documents were released as part of public records litigation.
The documents, which were turned over to the group Democracy Forward, are further evidence
that the Department of Homeland Security is spending a lot of resources to try to find
voter fraud.
The agency has developed new tools to comb through voter rolls, looking specifically
for non-citizen voters.
And one newly public report says DHS is in possession of close to 100 million voter records.
Multiple documents also note that the government has investigated nonprofits that register voters.
At one point, ICE even considered using undercover agents to support
investigative efforts in the field.
Despite the investigative energy being put toward the issue, no evidence has ever been
uncovered that non-citizen voting is a regular occurrence in American elections.
Miles Parks, NPR News, Washington.
Student protests continue throughout France today.
That is, despite the French prime minister's efforts to calm tensions,
he gave an address to the French nation yesterday.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports from Paris, the student protests are widening
with a movement of youth solidarity.
Students from the elite University of Sciences Po in Paris have now joined the high schooler's
protest movement and have barricaded a street in downtown Paris.
19-year-old Clara Usant says France's education system is not egalitarian
and the police are even more violent with young people in the suburbs.
I mean, everyone's seen the pictures of students in poorer neighborhoods getting beaten up.
We're actually physically attacked by the police.
Here, usually when we do a blockade, police don't get very violent.
So we wanted to show solidarity because we're in a privileged position.
She says they won't stop until the government agrees to spend money
to reduce inequalities in education.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
It's NPR.
Saudi Arabia says that two of its airports have been attacked this week
and three people have been killed.
More than 30 others have been wounded.
Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen are claiming responsibility.
Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed fighters are battling for territory in Yemen.
New polling shows that support for Medicare for All
is at the highest it's been in at least a decade.
Kate Wells with our partner KFF Health News reports from Lansing, Michigan.
If you go to one of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El Sayed's town halls in Michigan,
you will hear the crowd chant the campaign slogan.
Money out of.
Money in your.
Medicare for.
Two in three Americans now say they favor Medicare for All,
according to polling from KFF, a health policy research organization.
But many of them don't actually know what it means
and that support fluctuates based on what pollsters told them about it.
Medicare for All usually means a single insurance program
run by the federal government that replaces or radically changes private insurance.
Opponents argue that Medicare for All would raise taxes
and could lead to treatment delays.
That's Kate Wells from our partner KFF Health News.
The winner of this year's Nobel Prize in Literature is Canadian author Anne Carson.
She is a poet, essayist, and professor of classics.
The Nobel Committee pointed to Carson's use of ancient Greek and Roman themes for her works.
Tomorrow, the renowned Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.

topics.text: Democrats and Republicans spend heavily in House districts Trump won in 2024, making dozens of races newly competitive
Federal government investigated nonprofit voter registration groups as part of Trump's search for election crimes
Department of Homeland Security developed tools to search voter rolls for non-citizens, possesses nearly 100 million voter records
Student protests continue throughout France with elite university students joining high school movement, demanding education funding
Saudi Arabia says two airports attacked this week by Houthi rebels, killing three and wounding over thirty
Polling shows support for Medicare for All at highest level in at least a decade
Canadian author Anne Carson wins 2024 Nobel Prize in Literature for use of ancient Greek and Roman themes
